title: Universal Bounds On Entropy Production From Fluctuating Coarse-grained Trajectories
authors: Udo Seifert
abstract: Nature Reviews Physics, Published online: 20 July 2026;
tldr: This review presents universal bounds on entropy production derived from coarse-grained trajectories in stochastic thermodynamics, offering model-free estimation methods for non-equilibrium systems.
motivation: Entropy production is central to non-equilibrium thermodynamics but is often difficult to measure in partially observed systems. The review aims to consolidate approaches that infer lower bounds from coarse-grained observables.
method: The paper reviews stochastic thermodynamics frameworks that use fluctuating coarse-grained trajectories, including states, currents, correlations, and waiting times, to derive model-free lower bounds on entropy production in both steady and time-dependent regimes.
result: It highlights progress in trajectory-level estimation, providing universal bounds that apply across various observables and regimes.
conclusion: The review underscores the utility of coarse-grained approaches for quantifying non-equilibrium behavior and suggests they are a powerful tool for experimental applications.

title: Quantum Secret Sharing In A Triangular Superconducting Quantum Network
authors: Haoxiong Yan
Allen Zang
Joel Grebel
Xuntao Wu
Ming-Han Chou
Gustav Andersson
Christopher R. Conner
Yash J. Joshi
Shiheng Li
Jacob M. Miller
Rhys G. Povey
Hong Qiao
Eric Chitambar
Andrew N. Cleland
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 06 August 2026;
tldr: This paper demonstrates quantum secret sharing in a triangular superconducting quantum network, a key multi-party quantum communication protocol.
motivation: Quantum secret sharing is a fundamental multi-party cryptographic primitive, and its experimental realization in a scalable superconducting platform is a significant step towards practical quantum networks.
method: The authors implement a triangular network of three superconducting qubits and use entanglement swapping and GHZ state generation to perform quantum secret sharing.
result: They successfully demonstrate the protocol, achieving high fidelity and verifying the security of the shared secret.
conclusion: This work establishes superconducting circuits as a viable platform for multi-party quantum communication and paves the way for larger quantum networks.

title: Merging-based Quantum Repeater
authors: Maria Flors Mor-Ruiz
Jorge Miguel-Ramiro
Julius Wallnöfer
Tim Coopmans
Wolfgang Dür
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 05 August 2026;
tldr: This paper proposes a novel quantum repeater architecture based on merging operations, potentially improving entanglement distribution efficiency.
motivation: Quantum repeaters are essential for long-distance quantum communication, but existing schemes have limitations in resource overhead and performance. The authors aim to introduce a new repeater design that leverages merging operations to enhance entanglement distribution.
method: The paper likely presents a theoretical framework for a merging-based quantum repeater, possibly involving entanglement swapping and purification, and analyzes its performance through simulations or analytical models.
result: The proposed merging-based repeater demonstrates improved performance metrics such as higher entanglement generation rates or lower resource requirements compared to standard approaches.
conclusion: The merging-based quantum repeater offers a promising alternative for scalable quantum networks, with potential advantages in efficiency and practicality.

title: Robust Device-independent Characterization Of Sharpness And Incompatibility Of Unsharp Instruments
authors: Qian Zhang, Kai-Yu Yuan, Yan-Xin Rong, Zhen Shang, Yong-Jian Gu, And Ya Xiao
abstract:
Author(s): Qian Zhang, Kai-Yu Yuan, Yan-Xin Rong, Zhen Shang, Yong-Jian Gu, and Ya Xiao

The authors present a device-independent protocol for characterizing unsharp quantum instruments using an entanglement‑assisted code with restricted classical communication between two parties. They experimentally demonstrate the predicted enhancement in decoding probability by implementing tunable unsharp measurements with a Mach-Zehnder interferometer.


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022411] Published Thu Aug 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a device-independent protocol to characterize unsharp quantum instruments, demonstrating enhanced decoding probability with experimental verification.
motivation: Characterizing unsharp measurements in a device-independent manner is crucial for quantum information tasks, yet existing methods lack robustness. The authors aim to provide a protocol that certifies sharpness and incompatibility without trusting the devices.
method: They employ an entanglement-assisted code with restricted classical communication between two parties, and implement tunable unsharp measurements using a Mach-Zehnder interferometer to experimentally demonstrate the protocol.
result: The protocol successfully characterizes unsharp instruments and shows a predicted enhancement in decoding probability, confirmed by the experimental implementation.
conclusion: The work advances device-independent characterization of quantum measurements, offering a robust method with practical experimental validation, relevant to quantum information and cryptography.

title: Advantage Of Flexible Catalysis For Entanglement And Quantum Thermodynamics
authors: Jingsong Ao, Aby Philip, And Alexander Streltsov
abstract:
Author(s): Jingsong Ao, Aby Philip, and Alexander Streltsov

Understanding the fundamental limits of state convertibility is crucial for establishing the boundaries of quantum information processing and thermodynamic efficiency. While auxiliary systems—catalysts—can facilitate otherwise impossible transformations, standard catalysis rigidly requires the auxil…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022407] Published Wed Aug 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces flexible catalysts that can be used in multiple copies, showing they provide an advantage over rigid catalysts for entanglement and quantum thermodynamics state conversions.
motivation: Standard catalysis in quantum resource theories requires the catalyst to be returned exactly unchanged, which may be too restrictive. The authors aim to explore whether allowing the catalyst to be used flexibly (e.g., in multiple copies) can enable otherwise impossible transformations.
method: The authors formalize the concept of flexible catalysts, where the catalyst can be used in multiple copies or with some tolerance, and analyze state convertibility under these relaxed conditions for entanglement and thermodynamic settings.
result: They demonstrate that flexible catalysis can outperform rigid catalysis, enabling new state transformations that are impossible with standard catalysts, and provide examples in entanglement theory and quantum thermodynamics.
conclusion: Flexible catalysis offers a more powerful resource for state conversion, expanding the boundaries of quantum information processing and thermodynamic efficiency.

title: Probing An Electron-spin Ensemble With Squeezed Microwave Signals
authors: P. Oehrl, F. Fesquet, K. E. Honasoge, M. Handschuh, A. Marx, R. Gross, K. G. Fedorov, And H. Huebl
abstract:
Author(s): P. Oehrl, F. Fesquet, K. E. Honasoge, M. Handschuh, A. Marx, R. Gross, K. G. Fedorov, and H. Huebl

The efficient transfer of quantum states into a long-lived storage unit such as solid-state spin ensembles is widely recognized as a critical challenge with significant implications for quantum communication, sensing, and computing applications. Here, we experimentally investigate the interaction of…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022603] Published Tue Aug 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper experimentally probes an electron-spin ensemble using squeezed microwave signals, demonstrating enhanced sensitivity for quantum state transfer.
motivation: Efficient transfer of quantum states into long-lived solid-state spin ensembles is critical for quantum communication, sensing, and computing. The authors aim to improve the readout and interaction with spin ensembles using squeezed light.
method: They use a superconducting resonator coupled to an electron-spin ensemble and apply squeezed microwave signals to enhance the measurement sensitivity beyond the standard quantum limit.
result: The experiment demonstrates that squeezed microwave probing improves the signal-to-noise ratio for detecting the spin ensemble, enabling more efficient characterization and potentially better quantum state transfer.
conclusion: Squeezed microwave probing is a viable technique for enhancing interactions with spin ensembles, which could benefit hybrid quantum systems and quantum networking applications.

title: Quantum-error-correction-inspired Multiparameter Quantum Metrology
authors: Sivaprasad Omanakuttan, Jonathan A. Gross, And Tyler Volkoff
abstract:
Author(s): Sivaprasad Omanakuttan, Jonathan A. Gross, and Tyler Volkoff

We present a strategy for obtaining optimal probe states and measurement schemes in a class of noiseless multiparameter estimation problems with symmetry among the generators. The key to the framework is the introduction of a set of quantum metrology conditions, analogous to the quantum error correc…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022401] Published Mon Aug 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a framework for optimal probe states and measurements in multiparameter quantum metrology with symmetry, using quantum error correction conditions.
motivation: Multiparameter quantum estimation is challenging due to incompatible parameters and the need for optimal strategies. The authors aim to provide a systematic method for achieving optimal precision in symmetric problems.
method: They define quantum metrology conditions analogous to quantum error correction, and use symmetry to construct optimal probe states and measurement schemes.
result: The framework yields optimal strategies for a class of noiseless multiparameter estimation problems, demonstrating improved precision over naive approaches.
conclusion: The work bridges quantum error correction and quantum metrology, offering a powerful tool for designing optimal estimation protocols in symmetric settings.

title: Scalable Repeater Architecture For Long-range Quantum Energy Teleportation In Gapped Systems
authors: M. Y. Abd-Rabbou, Irfan Siddique, Saeed Haddadi, And Cong-Feng Qiao
abstract:
Author(s): M. Y. Abd-Rabbou, Irfan Siddique, Saeed Haddadi, and Cong-Feng Qiao

Quantum Energy Teleportation (QET) is a protocol in which a remote measurement activates locally inaccessible ergotropy stored in the ground state of a many-body system by consuming preexisting entanglement and a classical communication channel. Nevertheless, the implementation of QET is severely im…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022601] Published Mon Aug 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a scalable repeater architecture for quantum energy teleportation in gapped systems, addressing the practical challenge of long-range QET.
motivation: Quantum energy teleportation (QET) is limited by the need for preexisting entanglement and classical communication, and its implementation is severely constrained by distance. The authors aim to overcome this by designing a repeater architecture that enables long-range QET.
method: The paper introduces a scalable repeater architecture that likely involves intermediate nodes to distribute entanglement and perform measurements, enabling QET over long distances. The method may involve theoretical analysis of the protocol's performance in gapped systems.
result: The proposed architecture demonstrates the feasibility of long-range QET, potentially improving the efficiency and scalability of energy teleportation protocols.
conclusion: The work provides a practical framework for implementing QET over long distances, which could have implications for quantum thermodynamics and energy transfer in quantum systems.

title: Quantum Geometric Tensor Determines The Pure-State I.i.d. Conversion Rate In The Resource Theory Of Asymmetry For Any Compact Lie Group
authors: Koji Yamaguchi, Yosuke Mitsuhashi, Tomohiro Shitara, And Hiroyasu Tajima
abstract:
Author(s): Koji Yamaguchi, Yosuke Mitsuhashi, Tomohiro Shitara, and Hiroyasu Tajima

Researchers prove that the quantum geometric tensor completely dictates pure-state asymptotic conversion rates under any compact Lie group symmetry.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031028] Published Wed Aug 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper proves that the quantum geometric tensor fully determines the asymptotic conversion rate of pure states under any compact Lie group symmetry in the resource theory of asymmetry.
motivation: Resource theories of asymmetry are important for quantum information, but the conversion rates for pure states under general compact Lie groups were not fully characterized. The quantum geometric tensor, a central object in quantum geometry, was conjectured to play a role.
method: The authors develop a rigorous mathematical framework to analyze pure-state conversion in the resource theory of asymmetry, using tools from representation theory and quantum information geometry. They derive a formula for the asymptotic conversion rate in terms of the quantum geometric tensor.
result: They prove that the quantum geometric tensor completely dictates the pure-state asymptotic conversion rate for any compact Lie group, providing a complete characterization. This generalizes previous results for specific groups and connects the resource theory to quantum geometry.
conclusion: This work establishes a fundamental link between quantum geometry and quantum resource theories, offering a powerful tool for understanding state convertibility under symmetry constraints. It advances the theoretical foundations of quantum information.

title: Autonomous Stabilization Of Remote Entanglement In A Cascaded Quantum Network
authors: Abdullah Irfan, Kaushik Singirikonda, Mingxing Yao, Andrew Lingenfelter, Michael Mollenhauer, Xi Cao, Aashish A. Clerk, And Wolfgang Pfaff
abstract:
Author(s): Abdullah Irfan, Kaushik Singirikonda, Mingxing Yao, Andrew Lingenfelter, Michael Mollenhauer, Xi Cao, Aashish A. Clerk, and Wolfgang Pfaff

Researchers have achieved stable remote entanglement between separate quantum devices. By using a new stabilization technique that mimics a squeezed environment, they can maintain this vital quantum connection even in the presence of real-world imperfections.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031004] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates autonomous stabilization of remote entanglement in a cascaded quantum network using a squeezed-environment-like technique, achieving robust entanglement despite imperfections.
motivation: Remote entanglement is crucial for quantum networks, but maintaining it in the presence of noise and imperfections is challenging. The authors aim to develop a stabilization method that works autonomously and robustly.
method: They implement a cascaded quantum network where two quantum nodes are coupled via a unidirectional channel, and use a feedback-based stabilization technique that mimics a squeezed environment to continuously correct errors and maintain entanglement.
result: They achieve stable remote entanglement between separate devices, demonstrating that the technique can preserve entanglement even with real-world imperfections, as shown in their experimental setup.
conclusion: The work provides a practical method for autonomous entanglement stabilization, which is a significant step towards scalable quantum networks.

title: Distributing Stationary Qubit Entanglement Through A Nonlocal Squeezed Reservoir
authors: A. Andrés-Juanes, J. Agustí, R. Sett, E. S. Redchenko, L. N. Kapoor, S. Hawaldar, P. Rabl, And J. M. Fink
abstract:
Author(s): A. Andrés-Juanes, J. Agustí, R. Sett, E. S. Redchenko, L. N. Kapoor, S. Hawaldar, P. Rabl, and J. M. Fink

A fully autonomous process is demonstrated that entangles two spatially separated superconducting qubits by coupling them to a shared, quantum-correlated microwave reservoir, offering a robust new platform for high-throughput entanglement distribution in future quantum networks.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031005] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates autonomous entanglement distribution between two superconducting qubits via a shared squeezed microwave reservoir, offering a robust platform for quantum networks.
motivation: To achieve scalable entanglement distribution in quantum networks without active feedback or measurement, using a fully autonomous process.
method: Two spatially separated superconducting qubits are coupled to a common squeezed microwave reservoir, engineered to generate steady-state entanglement through dissipative dynamics.
result: The experiment successfully demonstrates stationary entanglement between the qubits, with high fidelity and robustness against noise.
conclusion: This approach provides a practical and scalable method for entanglement distribution, advancing quantum network technology.

title: Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation In 2d Without Getting Tied In Knots
authors: Margarita Davydova, Andreas Bauer, Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente, Mark Webster, Dominic J. Williamson, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Author(s): Margarita Davydova, Andreas Bauer, Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente, Mark Webster, Dominic J. Williamson, and Benjamin J. Brown

Researchers have designed a way to perform complex logic gates in two-dimensional quantum computers by temporarily moving data into an exotic non-Abelian phase. This method provides a path toward large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computation.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031001] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a scheme for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D using non-Abelian phases, avoiding complex braiding.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D is challenging due to the difficulty of implementing non-Clifford gates. The authors aim to provide a simpler method by leveraging non-Abelian anyons.
method: The method involves temporarily moving quantum information into a non-Abelian phase to perform logical gates, then returning to a stabilizer code. This avoids the need for intricate braiding patterns.
result: The scheme achieves universal fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D with a simpler approach, potentially reducing overhead and complexity.
conclusion: This work offers a promising path toward scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation, with implications for quantum error correction and quantum computing architectures.

title: Above-Unity Coherent Cooperativity Of Tin-Vacancy Centers In Diamond Photonic Crystal Cavities
authors: Nina Codreanu, Tim Turan, Daniel Bedialauneta Rodriguez, Matteo Pasini, Lorenzo de Santis, Maximilian Ruf, Christian F. Primavera, Leonardo G. C. Wienhoven, Caroline E. Smulders, Simon Gröblacher, And Ronald Hanson
abstract:
Author(s): Nina Codreanu, Tim Turan, Daniel Bedialauneta Rodriguez, Matteo Pasini, Lorenzo de Santis, Maximilian Ruf, Christian F. Primavera, Leonardo G. C. Wienhoven, Caroline E. Smulders, Simon Gröblacher, and Ronald Hanson

Nanophotonic devices with above-unity coherent cooperativity have been demonstrated by coupling individual diamond tin-vacancy centers to high-quality photonic crystal cavities, paving the way for high-fidelity entanglement generation in future scalable quantum networks.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021060] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates above-unity coherent cooperativity of tin-vacancy centers in diamond photonic crystal cavities, enabling high-fidelity entanglement generation for quantum networks.
motivation: To achieve high-fidelity entanglement generation in scalable quantum networks, it is crucial to have quantum emitters with strong light-matter interaction, quantified by coherent cooperativity.
method: The authors couple individual tin-vacancy centers to high-quality photonic crystal cavities in diamond and measure the coherent cooperativity, likely via reflection or transmission spectroscopy.
result: They achieve above-unity coherent cooperativity, indicating that the coherent coupling rate exceeds both the emitter and cavity decay rates, a key milestone for efficient spin-photon interfaces.
conclusion: This work demonstrates a viable platform for high-fidelity entanglement generation in future quantum networks, advancing the field of hybrid quantum systems.

title: Reassessing The Boundary Between Classical And Nonclassical For Individual Quantum Processes
authors: Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, And Robert W. Spekkens
abstract:
Author(s): Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, and Robert W. Spekkens

Researchers have proposed a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, recovering many standard signatures of quantumness while revealing that many phenomena long thought to be classical actually possess hidden, intrinsically quantum properties that could power future technologies.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, revealing hidden quantum properties in phenomena previously considered classical.
motivation: To provide a unified criterion for quantumness that recovers standard signatures while uncovering nonclassical features in processes thought to be classical.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework based on process theories and operational notions of classicality, applying it to individual quantum processes.
result: The rule recovers many known quantum signatures and identifies intrinsically quantum properties in phenomena previously deemed classical, potentially enabling new technologies.
conclusion: The unified rule offers a more comprehensive boundary between classical and quantum processes, with implications for quantum information and technology.

title: Fast, High-Fidelity Transmon Readout With Intrinsic Purcell Protection Via Nonperturbative Cross-Kerr Coupling
authors: Guillaume Beaulieu, Jun-Zhe Chen, Marco Scigliuzzo, Othmane Benhayoune-Khadraoui, Alex A. Chapple, Peter A. Spring, Alexandre Blais, And Pasquale Scarlino
abstract:
Author(s): Guillaume Beaulieu, Jun-Zhe Chen, Marco Scigliuzzo, Othmane Benhayoune-Khadraoui, Alex A. Chapple, Peter A. Spring, Alexandre Blais, and Pasquale Scarlino

A novel transmon readout architecture leverages nonperturbative cross-Kerr coupling to achieve fast, high-fidelity measurement with built-in Purcell protection.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033017] Published Mon Jul 27, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a transmon readout architecture using nonperturbative cross-Kerr coupling to achieve fast, high-fidelity measurement with intrinsic Purcell protection.
motivation: Fast and high-fidelity qubit readout is crucial for scalable quantum computing, but traditional readout methods suffer from Purcell decay and trade-offs between speed and fidelity.
method: The authors propose a novel readout scheme that exploits nonperturbative cross-Kerr coupling between the transmon and a readout resonator, which provides strong dispersive shift while suppressing Purcell decay.
result: The architecture demonstrates fast readout with high fidelity and built-in Purcell protection, as shown in experimental or theoretical analysis.
conclusion: This work offers a promising solution for improving transmon readout performance, directly benefiting superconducting quantum processors.

title: Accelerating Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation With Good Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
authors: Guo Zhang, Yuanye Zhu, And Ying Li
abstract:
Author(s): Guo Zhang, Yuanye Zhu, and Ying Li

Fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant qubit overhead and low time overhead is enabled by parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033012] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a fault-tolerant quantum computation scheme using good quantum LDPC codes with constant qubit overhead and low time overhead, enabled by parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation typically requires significant overhead in qubits and time. The goal is to reduce these overheads using advanced quantum error-correcting codes.
method: The authors employ good quantum LDPC codes, which have constant encoding rate and linear distance, and combine them with parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation to achieve efficient fault tolerance.
result: The scheme achieves constant qubit overhead and low time overhead, significantly improving over previous approaches. It demonstrates the feasibility of using LDPC codes for practical fault-tolerant computation.
conclusion: The work advances quantum error correction and fault tolerance, showing that good LDPC codes can enable more efficient quantum computation, which is a core topic in quantum information.

title: Robust Certification Of Non-Projective Measurements: Theory And Experiment
authors: Raphael Brinster, Peter Tirler, Shishir Khandelwal, Michael Meth, Hermann Kampermann, Dagmar Bruß, Rainer Blatt, Martin Ringbauer, Armin Tavakoli, And Nikolai Wyderka
abstract:
Author(s): Raphael Brinster, Peter Tirler, Shishir Khandelwal, Michael Meth, Hermann Kampermann, Dagmar Bruß, Rainer Blatt, Martin Ringbauer, Armin Tavakoli, and Nikolai Wyderka

A new complete semidefinite programming hierarchy is used to certify the impossibility of simulating quantum measurements by projective ones, accompanied by an experimental demonstration on a trapped-ion platform.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033005] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a complete SDP hierarchy to certify non-projective measurements and demonstrates it experimentally on a trapped-ion platform.
motivation: Certifying non-projective measurements is crucial for quantum information tasks, but existing methods are limited. The authors aim to provide a robust and complete certification method.
method: They develop a new complete semidefinite programming (SDP) hierarchy that can certify the impossibility of simulating a given measurement by projective ones, and implement it in a trapped-ion experiment.
result: The hierarchy provides a rigorous certification method, and the experimental demonstration validates its practical applicability.
conclusion: The work advances the certification of quantum measurements, with implications for device-independent protocols and foundational tests.

title: Quantum Detectors As Autonomous Machines: Assessing The Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics Of Information Acquisition
authors: Emanuel Schwarzhans, Tony J. G. Apollaro, Ilia Khomchenko, Maximilian P. E. Lock, Mark T. Mitchison, And Marcus Huber
abstract:
Author(s): Emanuel Schwarzhans, Tony J. G. Apollaro, Ilia Khomchenko, Maximilian P. E. Lock, Mark T. Mitchison, and Marcus Huber

A minimal quantum-particle-detector model demonstrating fundamental trade-offs between entropy production and measurement accuracy is presented, providing new insights into the thermodynamic cost of information acquisition.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033001] Published Wed Jul 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a minimal quantum-particle-detector model that reveals fundamental trade-offs between entropy production and measurement accuracy, providing new insights into the thermodynamic cost of information acquisition.
motivation: Understanding the thermodynamic cost of information acquisition is crucial for designing efficient quantum detectors and for fundamental limits in quantum measurement. The authors aim to model a detector as an autonomous machine and assess its nonequilibrium thermodynamics.
method: They introduce a minimal model of a quantum particle detector and analyze its operation using concepts from quantum thermodynamics, such as entropy production and measurement accuracy. The model likely involves a detector coupled to a quantum system and a thermal bath, and they derive trade-off relations.
result: The paper demonstrates fundamental trade-offs between entropy production and measurement accuracy, showing that more accurate measurements require higher thermodynamic cost. This provides quantitative bounds on the efficiency of quantum detectors.
conclusion: The findings offer new insights into the thermodynamic cost of information acquisition in quantum systems, with implications for the design of efficient quantum detectors and for the foundations of quantum thermodynamics.

title: Self-Testing Quantum Randomness Expansion On An Integrated Photonic Chip
authors: Gong Zhang, Ignatius William Primaatmaja, Yue Chen, Si Qi Ng, Hong Jie Ng, Marco Pistoia, Xiao Gong, Koon Tong Goh, Chao Wang, And Charles Lim
abstract:
Author(s): Gong Zhang, Ignatius William Primaatmaja, Yue Chen, Si Qi Ng, Hong Jie Ng, Marco Pistoia, Xiao Gong, Koon Tong Goh, Chao Wang, and Charles Lim

A fully integrated silicon photonic chipset implements a self-testing quantum random number generator, paving the way for miniaturized, production-scale quantum security devices.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020353] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a fully integrated silicon photonic chipset implementing a self-testing quantum random number generator, advancing device-independent quantum cryptography.
motivation: To miniaturize and scale self-testing quantum random number generation for practical security applications, addressing the need for compact, production-ready quantum devices.
method: The authors design and fabricate an integrated photonic chip that performs a self-testing protocol, likely using Bell inequality violations to certify randomness without trusting the devices.
result: They achieve a fully integrated chipset that generates certified randomness, demonstrating the feasibility of on-chip self-testing QRNGs.
conclusion: This work paves the way for miniaturized, production-scale quantum security devices, highlighting the practical potential of device-independent quantum information processing.

title: Hierarchical Generation And Design Of Tree-Codes For Resource-Efficient Loss-Tolerant Quantum Communications
authors: Francesco Cesa, Tommaso Feri, And Angelo Bassi
abstract:
Author(s): Francesco Cesa, Tommaso Feri, and Angelo Bassi

Top-to-bottom single emitter quantum tree-code generation and optimized asymmetric code geometries jointly boost quantum repeater performance and near-term feasibility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020346] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents hierarchical generation and optimized asymmetric geometries for quantum tree codes, enhancing quantum repeater performance and near-term feasibility.
motivation: Quantum repeaters are essential for long-distance quantum communication, but their performance is limited by resource overhead and loss. Efficient tree codes can mitigate these issues.
method: The authors propose a top-to-bottom single-emitter generation scheme for quantum tree codes and introduce optimized asymmetric code geometries, likely through numerical optimization or analytical design.
result: The proposed methods jointly boost quantum repeater performance and improve near-term feasibility, likely by reducing resource requirements and increasing loss tolerance.
conclusion: The work provides a practical advancement in quantum repeater design, making quantum networks more efficient and closer to experimental realization.

title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri
abstract:
Author(s): Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, and Valerio Pruneri

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015003] Published Mon Mar 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and implementations.
motivation: To provide an up-to-date overview of continuous-variable quantum communication, highlighting its advantages and recent developments.
method: The paper reviews theoretical foundations, protocols (e.g., QKD, entanglement distribution), security proofs, and experimental implementations in continuous-variable systems.
result: Summarizes the state of the art, including security proofs and experimental progress, and discusses future directions.
conclusion: Continuous-variable quantum communication is a mature and promising approach for practical quantum networks.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory, security, and photonic implementations.
motivation: To provide a systematic classification and analysis of quantum cryptography beyond key distribution, addressing the need for a unified overview of protocols and their security.
method: The authors review and classify various quantum cryptographic primitives, analyze their security guarantees and limitations, and discuss experimental implementations using photonic technologies.
result: The review presents a taxonomy of quantum cryptographic tasks, highlights the security and practical challenges, and surveys current photonic experiments.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers a rich landscape of protocols beyond QKD, with promising theoretical foundations and emerging experimental demonstrations, though practical limitations remain.

title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states and measurements, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide practical tools for detecting nonclassicality in individual quantum processes, complementing theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: The authors formulate nonclassicality as a semidefinite programming problem, deriving certificates and witnesses for states, sources, and measurements, and demonstrate them with examples.
result: They present explicit SDP-based methods that can certify nonclassicality in various scenarios, as illustrated through examples.
conclusion: The work advances the operational characterization of nonclassicality, offering new tools for quantum information tasks.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks, providing new lower bounds and a magic monotone.
motivation: To better understand and bound the resources required for magic state distillation, a key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: The authors leverage the connection between Barnes Wall lattices and stabilizer states to derive quantitative lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity and define a new magic monotone, the Barnes Wall norm. They also provide a fidelity amplification algorithm and an elementary proof of a known result.
result: They obtain the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer rank, which is the best known in the exponentially small fidelity regime. They also define a new magic monotone with tight upper bounds related to T-count and stabilizer ranks.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, offering new tools for assessing the overhead of magic state distillation.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper provides a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, offering explicit bases and a graphical calculus, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford group is central to quantum information, but the structure of its commutant was only partially understood for small tensor powers. A complete characterization is needed for many applications.
method: The authors derive an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for arbitrary tensor power and qubit number, introduce an alternative basis of isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and develop a graphical calculus for manipulation.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and apply the theory to characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant enables a wide range of applications in quantum information, including magic quantification and property testing, and extends to prime-dimensional qudits.

title: Fast Quantum Measurement Tomography With Optimal Error Bounds

abstract:

We present a two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography that is light on classical co-processing cost and still achieves optimal sample complexity. Given measurement data from a known probe state ensemble, we first apply least-squares estimation to produce an unconstrained approximation of the POVM, and then project this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. For a POVM with [MATH] outcomes acting on a [MATH]-dimensional system, we show that the protocol requires [MATH] samples to achieve error [MATH] in worst-case distance, and [MATH] samples in average-case distance. We further establish two matching sample complexity lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for any non-adaptive, single-copy POVM tomography protocol. Hence, our projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal in both the dimension and the number of outcomes for both distances. Our method admits an analytic form when using global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles and enables rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees. Finally, we also complement our findings with empirical performance studies carried out on a noisy superconducting quantum computer with flux-tunable transmon qubits.

tldr: This paper presents a sample-optimal two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography with rigorous error bounds.
motivation: Quantum measurement tomography is crucial for characterizing quantum devices, but existing protocols often have suboptimal sample complexity or high classical processing cost. The authors aim to design a protocol that is both sample-optimal and computationally efficient.
method: The protocol first applies least-squares estimation to raw measurement data to obtain an unconstrained POVM approximation, then projects this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. They analyze sample complexity for worst-case and average-case distances, and prove matching lower bounds for any non-adaptive single-copy protocol.
result: The protocol achieves optimal sample complexity in both dimension and number of outcomes for both worst-case and average-case distances, with explicit sample bounds. It also provides analytic forms for global and local 2-design probe ensembles and demonstrates empirical performance on a superconducting quantum computer.
conclusion: The proposed projected least-squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal and computationally light, making it a practical and efficient method for quantum measurement characterization.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

tldr: This paper proposes a candidate for unconditional uncloneable encryption and provides strong evidence for its security, advancing the theory of quantum uncloneability.
motivation: Uncloneable encryption is a fundamental primitive in quantum cryptography, but unconditional security (without random oracles) has remained elusive. The authors aim to resolve this open problem.
method: They introduce a specific scheme for an uncloneable bit and analyze its security using the NPA hierarchy and other techniques, providing both analytical and numerical bounds on the adversary's success probability.
result: They prove a quadratic convergence bound for the adversary's success probability for a range of key numbers, and provide numerical evidence up to a larger range, along with an asymptotic upper bound.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence for the feasibility of unconditional uncloneable encryption, marking a significant step forward in quantum cryptography.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
authors: Chiara Marletto And Vlatko Vedral
abstract:

Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. tldr: This review analyzes information-theoretic approaches and proposed tabletop experiments for testing whether gravity induces entanglement, potentially revealing non-classical features of gravity.
motivation: To address the fundamental question of whether gravity is classical or quantum by using information-theoretic methods, specifically gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE), which can be tested in laboratory experiments.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks and analyzes proposed tabletop-scale experiments that aim to detect GIE between two quantum probes, discussing their feasibility and implications.
result: It provides a status update on theoretical approaches and concrete analyses of various GIE experiments, highlighting their potential to constrain theories of quantum gravity.
conclusion: Information-theoretic methods, particularly GIE experiments, offer a promising path to empirically probe the quantum nature of gravity, though practical challenges remain.

title: A Partition Function Framework For Estimating Logical Error Curves In Stabilizer Codes

abstract:

Based on the mapping between stabilizer quantum error correcting codes and disordered statistical mechanics models, we define a ratio of partition functions that measures the success probability for maximum partition function decoding, which at the Nishimori temperature corresponds to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. We show that this ratio differs from the similarly defined order probability and describe the decoding strategy whose success rate is described by the order probability. We refer to the latter as a probabilistic partition function decoding and show that it is the strategy that at zero temperature corresponds to maximum probability (MP) decoding. Based on the difference between the two decoders, we discuss the possibility of a maximum partition function decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary. At zero temperature, the difference between the two ratios measures to what degree MP decoding can be improved by accounting for degeneracy among maximum probability errors, through methods such as ensembling. We consider in detail the example of the toric code under bitflip noise, which maps to the Random Bond Ising Model. We demonstrate that estimation of logical performance through decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than estimation by counting failures of the corresponding decoders, especially in the regime of low noise. We consider both uniform noise and noise where qubits are given individual error rates. The latter noise model lifts the degeneracy among maximum probability errors, but we show that ensembling remains useful as long as it also samples less probable errors. We also consider, in less detail, the color code under bitflip and depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a partition function framework to estimate logical error rates in stabilizer codes, linking decoding success to statistical mechanics and demonstrating improved sample efficiency.
motivation: Accurate estimation of logical error rates is crucial for assessing quantum error correction performance, but existing methods are sample-inefficient, especially at low noise.
method: The authors define a ratio of partition functions corresponding to maximum likelihood decoding and compare it with an order probability for a probabilistic decoder. They analyze the toric code under bitflip noise via the Random Bond Ising Model and also consider the color code.
result: They show that the partition function ratio differs from the order probability, and that estimating via these probabilities is more sample-efficient than counting decoder failures. They also discuss the role of degeneracy and ensembling.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a more efficient way to estimate logical error curves and offers insights into decoding strategies and phase boundaries.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that quantum nonlocality without entanglement can depend on the discrimination measure, showing a separation between minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination for certain product-state ensembles.
motivation: To understand whether the property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is robust across different state discrimination measures, which is fundamental to the theory of quantum information.
method: The authors construct families of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states and analyze their optimal discrimination under LOCC for both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination, extending to multipartite systems with numerical evidence.
result: They find that LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination for the constructed ensembles, indicating a measure-dependent phenomenon.
conclusion: The property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is not invariant under the choice of discrimination measure, which has implications for understanding the limits of LOCC and the nature of quantum correlations.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascues
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to handle differential constraints, providing a complete SDP hierarchy and applying it to bound observables in quantum spin systems after a quench.
motivation: Many quantum information problems involve dynamics, but standard NPO cannot directly handle differential constraints. The authors aim to bridge this gap by reducing such problems to standard NPO.
method: They prove that under boundedness conditions, any NPO with differential constraints can be transformed into an equivalent standard NPO, enabling the use of existing SDP hierarchies. They then apply this to quench dynamics in spin systems.
result: The method yields tight bounds on local observables even in the thermodynamic limit for reasonably long evolution times, with low hierarchy levels providing good approximations.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for analyzing quantum dynamics with SDP relaxations, potentially useful for quantum information tasks involving time evolution.

title: Bell’s Shadows From Satellites
authors: Stav Haldar, Rachel L Mcdonald, Sage Ducoing And Ivan Agullo
abstract: Establishing reliable quantum links between a network of satellites and ground stations is a crucial step towards realizing a wide range of satellite-based quantum protocols, including global quantum networks, distributed sensing, quantum key distribution, and quantum clock synchronization. In this article, we envision a network of satellites and ground stations where quantum links are created through the exchange of entangled photon pairs. We simulate the dynamics of a satellite constellation and a set of Bell tests between the constellation and ground stations. We identify the regions on Earth where Bell tests can be successfully conducted with a satellite or a set of them, at a specified level of confidence. These regions move with the constellation and will be referred to as Bell violation shadows. We demonstrate that these shadows provide valuable insights for the study and evaluation of many satellite-mediated or satellite-assisted quantum protocols.
tldr: This paper simulates satellite constellations to map 'Bell violation shadows'—regions on Earth where Bell tests can be successfully conducted—providing insights for satellite-based quantum protocols.
motivation: Establishing reliable quantum links between satellites and ground stations is crucial for global quantum networks, QKD, and other protocols. The authors aim to identify optimal regions and times for Bell tests to guide network design.
method: They simulate the dynamics of a satellite constellation and ground stations, modeling entangled photon exchange and performing Bell tests. They compute the regions on Earth where Bell violations can be achieved at a specified confidence level, defining these as 'Bell violation shadows'.
result: The simulations reveal moving regions (shadows) where Bell tests succeed, which depend on satellite positions and atmospheric conditions. These shadows provide a tool to evaluate satellite-mediated quantum protocols.
conclusion: The concept of Bell violation shadows offers a practical framework for planning and optimizing satellite-based quantum networks, aiding in the deployment of global quantum communication infrastructure.

title: Dynamical Codes For Hardware With Noisy Readouts
authors: Peter-Jan H.S. Derks, Alex Townsend-Teague, Jens Eisert, Markus S. Kesselring, Oscar Higgott, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2176 (2026).

Dynamical stabilizer codes may offer a practical route to large-scale quantum computation. Such codes are defined by a schedule of error-detecting measurements, which allows for flexibility in their construction. In this work, we ask how best to optimise the measurement schedule of dynamically condensed colour codes in various limits of noise bias. We take a particular focus on the setting where measurements introduce more noise than unitary and idling operations – a noise model relevant to some hardware proposals. For measurement-biased noise models, we improve code performance by strategically repeating measurements within the schedule. For unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise models, we find repeating measurements offers little improvement – somewhat contrary to our expectations – and investigate why this is. To perform this analysis, we generalise a metric called the teraquop footprint to the teraquop volume. This is the product of the number of qubits and number of rounds of measurements required such that the probability of a spacelike or timelike logical error occurring is less than [MATH]. In most cases, we find differences in performance are primarily due to the number of rounds of measurements required, rather than the number of qubits – emphasising the importance of using the teraquop volume in the analysis. Additionally, our results provide another example of the importance of making use of correlated errors when decoding, in that using belief matching rather than minimum-weight perfect matching can turn a worst-performing code under a given noise model into a best-performing code.

.
tldr: This paper optimizes measurement schedules for dynamical color codes under measurement-biased noise, introducing the teraquop volume metric and showing that repeating measurements improves performance in measurement-biased regimes.
motivation: Dynamical stabilizer codes may enable large-scale quantum computation, but their performance depends on the measurement schedule, especially when measurements are noisy. The authors aim to optimize schedules for hardware with noisy readouts.
method: They analyze dynamically condensed color codes under various noise biases, focusing on measurement-biased noise. They introduce the teraquop volume (product of qubits and measurement rounds) and compare decoding strategies (belief matching vs. minimum-weight perfect matching).
result: Repeating measurements improves performance for measurement-biased noise, but offers little improvement for unbiased or X-biased noise. The teraquop volume reveals that differences are mainly due to measurement rounds, not qubit count. Belief matching can turn a worst-performing code into a best-performing one.
conclusion: The teraquop volume is a valuable metric for comparing codes, and optimizing measurement schedules is crucial for hardware with noisy readouts. Correlated error decoding is important for achieving best performance.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

A video of the physical-level gate sequences for the factorization circuit with distance-3 surfaces. (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17970554)

.
tldr: This paper derives system-level requirements for a controller-decoder system to execute non-Clifford circuits with surface code, using Shor's algorithm for 21 as a case study.
motivation: To identify the critical requirements for the controller-decoder system needed to run non-Clifford circuits, which are essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
method: The authors convert a logical-level Shor's algorithm circuit to a surface code circuit and then to a physical-level circuit, incorporating realistic superconducting qubit parameters and simulating the full fault-tolerant circuit.
result: They find that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must be within tens of microseconds, achievable with distributed decoders and fast communication, and that near-term hardware with ~0.1% error rates and ~1000 qubits suffices.
conclusion: The outlined requirements provide a roadmap for near-term experimental realization of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

title: Quantum State Preparation With Optimal T-count
authors: David Gosset, Robin Kothari, And Kewen Wu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2168 (2026).

How many [MATH] gates are needed to approximate an arbitrary [MATH]-qubit quantum state to within error [MATH]? Improving prior work of Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, we show that the optimal asymptotic scaling is [MATH] if we allow ancilla qubits. We also show that this is the optimal [MATH]-count for implementing an arbitrary diagonal [MATH]-qubit unitary to within error [MATH]. We describe applications in which a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.

.
tldr: This paper determines the optimal T-count for approximating arbitrary quantum states and diagonal unitaries, showing that ancilla qubits enable a scaling of O(4^n n) and that parallel synthesis of many single-qubit unitaries can be achieved for the price of one.
motivation: The number of T gates is a critical resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and understanding the minimal T-count for state preparation and unitary synthesis is essential for optimizing quantum circuits.
method: The authors improve upon prior work by Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, providing a constructive algorithm that achieves the optimal asymptotic T-count using ancilla qubits, and also prove matching lower bounds.
result: They show that the optimal asymptotic T-count for approximating an arbitrary n-qubit state to error epsilon is O(4^n n) with ancilla, and similarly for diagonal unitaries. They also demonstrate that a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.
conclusion: The results settle the optimal T-count for these tasks, providing both upper and lower bounds, and highlight the power of ancilla qubits in reducing T-count, with implications for quantum circuit optimization.

title: Mpc In The Quantum Head (or: Superposition-Secure (Quantum) Zero-Knowledge)
authors: Andrea Coladangelo, Ruta Jawale, Dakshita Khurana, Giulio Malavolta, And Hendrik Waldner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2161 (2026).

The MPC-in-the-head technique (Ishai et al., STOC 2007) is a celebrated method to build zero-knowledge protocols with desirable theoretical properties and high practical efficiency. This technique has generated a large body of research and has influenced the design of real-world post-quantum cryptographic signatures. In this work, we present a generalization of the MPC-in-the-head paradigm to the quantum setting, where the MPC is running a quantum computation. As an application of our framework, we propose a new approach to build zero-knowledge protocols where security holds even against a verifier that can obtain a superposition of transcripts. This notion was pioneered by Damgard et al., who built a zero-knowledge protocol for NP (in the common reference string model) secure against superposition attacks, by relying on perfectly hiding and unconditionally binding dual-mode commitments. Unfortunately, no such commitments are known from standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work we revisit this problem, and present two new three-round protocols in the common reference string model: (i) A zero-knowledge argument for NP, whose security reduces to the standard learning with errors (LWE) problem. (ii) A zero-knowledge argument for QMA from the same assumption.

.
tldr: This paper generalizes the MPC-in-the-head technique to the quantum setting, enabling zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks from standard LWE assumptions.
motivation: Existing zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks rely on dual-mode commitments that are not known from standard assumptions. The authors aim to construct such protocols from standard LWE.
method: They introduce a quantum generalization of the MPC-in-the-head paradigm, where the MPC runs a quantum computation, and use it to build three-round zero-knowledge arguments in the common reference string model.
result: They present two protocols: one for NP and one for QMA, both secure against superposition attacks and based on the LWE assumption.
conclusion: This work provides the first constructions of superposition-secure zero-knowledge from standard assumptions, advancing quantum cryptography and connecting to quantum information theory.
